question.:question/problem:
Consider the curve defined parametrically by

$$
x=2 t - 2,\quad y=(t - 4) (t + 3),\quad t\in\mathbb{R}.
$$

The Cartesian equation is

$y=$ {{field-1}}$,\quad x\in\mathbb{R}.$
question.:question/worked-solution:
Eliminate the parameter by using the $x$ equation to isolate $t$:

$$
\begin{aligned}x &=2 t - 2 \\ t &=\frac{x}{2} + 1\end{aligned}
$$

Substitute $t=\frac{x}{2} + 1$ into the original $y$ expression, then simplify:

$$
\begin{aligned}y &=((\frac{x}{2} + 1) - 4) ((\frac{x}{2} + 1) + 3) \\ &=(\frac{x}{2} - 3) (\frac{x}{2} + 4) \\ &=\frac{(x - 6) (x + 8)}{4}\end{aligned}
$$

The affine $x$ equation attains every real value, so $x\in\mathbb{R}$.

Therefore the complete Cartesian equation is

$$
y=\frac{(x - 6) (x + 8)}{4},\quad x\in\mathbb{R}.
$$

question.:question/problem:
Consider the curve defined parametrically as

$$
x=2\sin t,\qquad y=\cos t-4,\qquad t\in[0,2\pi).
$$

The Cartesian equation of this curve is

{{field-1}}$=1.$
question.:question/worked-solution:
First, let's make the trigonometric functions the subject of each equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}
x=2\sin t & \Rightarrow\quad \sin t=\frac{x}{2} \\
y=\cos t-4 & \Rightarrow\quad \cos t=y + 4
\end{aligned}
$$

Using the Pythagorean identity $\sin^2 t+\cos^2 t=1$, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}
\left(\frac{x}{2}\right)^2+\left(y + 4\right)^2 & =1 \\
\frac{1}{4}x^2+\left(y + 4\right)^2 & =1.
\end{aligned}
$$

The traced curve also satisfies $-2\le x\le 2,\quad -5\le y\le -3$.

question.:question/problem:
Find the Cartesian equation of the curve defined parametrically as

$$
x=6\cot t,\qquad y=\csc t,\qquad 0<t<\frac{\pi}{2}.
$$
question.:question/worked-solution:
First, let's make the trigonometric functions the subject of each equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}
x=6\cot t & \Rightarrow\quad \cot t=\frac{x}{6} \\
y=\csc t & \Rightarrow\quad \csc t=y
\end{aligned}
$$

Dividing the Pythagorean identity $\sin^2 t+\cos^2 t=1$ by $\sin^2 t$, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}
\frac{\sin^2 t}{\sin^2 t}+\frac{\cos^2 t}{\sin^2 t} & =\frac{1}{\sin^2 t} \\
1+\left(\frac{\cos t}{\sin t}\right)^2 & =\left(\frac{1}{\sin t}\right)^2 \\
1+\cot^2 t & =\csc^2 t.
\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting $\cot t=\frac{x}{6}$ and $\csc t=y$ into this formula, we get

$$
1+\left(\frac{x}{6}\right)^2=y^2.
$$

So the Cartesian equation of the given curve is $y^2=1+\left(\frac{x}{6}\right)^2.$

Expanding the products or squaring the coordinate fractions gives

$$
y^{2}=\frac{x^{2}}{36} + 1.
$$

The traced curve also satisfies $x>0,\quad y>1$.

question.:question/problem:
Given that $f(x)=\left(3 x + 3\right)^{4}$, find $f^{\prime}(x).$

Use the decomposition $g(x)=3 x + 3$ and $F(u)=u^{4}$, so $f(x)=F(g(x))$. Recall that $f^{\prime}(x)=F^{\prime}(g(x))g^{\prime}(x)$.
question.:question/worked-solution:
Let $g(x)=3 x + 3$ and $F(g)=g^{4}$, so $f(x)=F(g(x))$.

Differentiating, we have

$$
\begin{aligned} F^{\prime}(g)&=4 g^{3}, \\ g^{\prime}(x)&=3.\end{aligned}
$$

Then, using the chain rule,

$$
\begin{aligned} f^{\prime}(x)&=F^{\prime}(g(x))\cdot g^{\prime}(x) \\ &=\left(4 \left(3 x + 3\right)^{3}\right)\cdot\left(3\right) \\ &=12 \left(3 x + 3\right)^{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

$$

$$

Take the cross partial derivatives, holding the other coordinates constant:

$$
\begin{aligned}R_y-Q_z&=\bigl(- 2 x - 2 y z\bigr)-\bigl(2 x z\bigr) \\ &=- 2 x z - 2 x - 2 y z \\ P_z-R_x&=\bigl(- 2 y\bigr)-\bigl(- 2 y - 2 z\bigr) \\ &=2 z \\ Q_x-P_y&=\bigl(- 2 x y + z^{2}\bigr)-\bigl(- 2 x y - 2 z\bigr) \\ &=z^{2} + 2 z\end{aligned}
$$

Thus

$$
\begin{aligned}\nabla\times\mathbf F&=-\bigl(2 x z + 2 x + 2 y z\bigr)\,\mathbf i \\ &\quad+2 z\,\mathbf j \\ &\quad+\bigl(z^{2} + 2 z\bigr)\,\mathbf k\end{aligned}
$$

$$

$$

Therefore

$$
(\nabla\times\mathbf F)(1,1,-1)=2\,\mathbf i-2\,\mathbf j-\,\mathbf k
$$
